title: Cooling the Urban Heat Island
paragraphs: On a hot summer evening, the centre of a large city can be up to ten degrees warmer than the farmland just outside it. This effect, known as the urban heat island, was first described in the early nineteenth century by Luke Howard, an amateur scientist who recorded temperatures in and around London. Today, with more than half of the world's population living in cities, and with heatwaves becoming more frequent, the problem is receiving more attention than ever before.

Several factors are responsible for the extra heat. Dark surfaces such as roads and roofs absorb sunlight during the day and release it slowly at night, which is why the difference between city and countryside is often greatest after sunset. Tall buildings trap warm air and reduce wind speeds, while the lack of plants means that there is less evaporation, a natural process that cools the air. In addition, cars, air conditioners and factories all produce heat directly.

The consequences are not simply a matter of comfort. High night-time temperatures make it difficult for the body to recover from the heat of the day, and they are strongly associated with an increase in deaths during heatwaves, particularly among elderly people. Higher temperatures also increase the demand for air conditioning, which uses large amounts of electricity and, in turn, releases more heat into the streets. Some studies suggest that the heat island effect can also make air pollution worse.

One of the simplest solutions is to change the colour of surfaces. Light-coloured materials reflect more sunlight and therefore stay cooler. In Los Angeles, the city has tested a grey-white coating on some streets, which reduced surface temperatures by several degrees. Cool roofs, painted white or covered with reflective materials, have been introduced in cities from New York to Ahmedabad in India. They are relatively cheap and can also lower the cost of cooling the buildings below them.

Many planners, however, believe that the most effective approach is to bring nature back into the city. Trees provide shade and cool the air through evaporation, and a single large tree can have a cooling effect similar to several air conditioners. Singapore, one of the most densely populated cities in the world, has made green space a central part of its planning, with gardens on roofs and plants growing up the walls of buildings. Parks, rivers and lakes can also create areas of cooler air that spread into the surrounding streets.

These solutions are not without difficulties. Trees take years to grow and need water, which may be in short supply in hot, dry regions. Reflective surfaces can create glare and, if they are poorly placed, may simply send heat towards nearby buildings. For this reason, experts recommend combining different methods and planning them carefully for local conditions. As cities continue to grow, the way they are designed may decide how comfortable, and how safe, life will be for billions of people.
